newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Stockholm bourse head sees Nordic cluster in 5 yrs.
newsitem.headline: Stockholm bourse head sees Nordic cluster in 5 yrs.

text.p: The first steps could be taken next year toward a Nordic-Baltic stock exchange cluster and a merger of Swedish stocks and derivatives trading, the head of the Stockholm Stock Exchange said on Wednesday.

Such a grouping would allow investors to deal on all the region's bourses from one trading location. "In five years we could have a Baltic cluster (consisting of the Nordic and Baltic countries) and (a merger)," Stockholm Stock Exchange head Bengt Ryden told Reuters in an interview.
"And the first steps in both areas (the cluster and the merger) are likely to be taken in 1997."
Ryden said he envisioned a common regional electronic network within the cluster, allowing local exchanges to stay in business.
The Stockholm Stock Exchange, which is by far the largest and most succesful bourse in the Nordic and Baltic region, is likely to be the cluster's hub, Ryden said.
"Stockholm has a very strong position already with a good financial infrastructure and strong competence regarding analysis, accountancy and advisory service."
Currently, the situation is exceptionally favourable for moving toward a cluster, he said.
"Oslo, Helsinki and Copenhagen have a unique opportunity as they are on the verge of making decisions about next generation trading systems."
But the heads of the Helsinki and Copenhagen exchanges have widely different opinions about a cluster.

In leading articles in Swedish newspaper Svenska Dagbladet in December, Denmark's Lars Johansen embraced Nordic cooperation, while Finland's Juhani Erma had several objections, but still kept the door ajar for cooperation.

Ryden called for patience and pointed to the Benelux countries, which already have plans for a cluster, and to other countries, such as France and Germany, which are probing cooperation possibilities.
"The Nordic, or Baltic, area is, however, a very natural region. And we have very good reasons to cooperate as each one of us is very small," he said.
A Nordic-Baltic region would be a large player in Europe, he said. When the clusters have been set up, Ryden forecast that they in turn may be linked.

Parallel to the Nordic and Baltic cluster development, Ryden expected a merger of the Stockholm Stock Exchange, the OM Group, which is active in derivatives trading, and Vardepapperscentralen (VPC), which deals with clearing and registration of Swedish share transactions.
"This would mean dynamic advantages because an integrated market probably is more attractive."
Current discussions concern what form such a merger would take, he said.
"There could be a common ownership for the three (the bourse, OM and VPC) in the future. And ownership cooperation usually facilitates integration," he said.
The three groups already have some owners in common and the state has indicated that it could sell its 50 percent VPC stake, Ryden added.
